## Answers

### T01 (in_scope): Can you explain murabahah in simple words?

**Expected key points:** Sale at disclosed cost plus profit; bank owns asset first; customer pays in instalments

**Retrieved:** IFC-008 (0.711), IFC-001 (0.622), IFC-010 (0.586)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> Murabahah is a sale. The bank buys an asset, then sells it to you at its original cost plus an agreed profit. The bank discloses both amounts, and you usually pay the total price in instalments.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: Murabahah (BNM/RH/STD 028-4, 23 Dec 2013); BNM Policy Document: Ijarah (28 Jun 2018) (Murabahah para 1.3-1.5; Ijarah para 8.1(a), 22.1-22.3)
> - BNM Policy Document: Murabahah (BNM/RH/STD 028-4, 23 Dec 2013) (Para 1.3-1.4, 10.1, 14.11-14.12)
> - BNM Policy Document: Mudarabah (BNM/RH/STD 028-8, 20 Apr 2015) (Para 10.1, 16.4, 17.1-17.2)

### T02 (in_scope): Is ijarah the same as murabahah?

**Expected key points:** No: ijarah is a lease (bank keeps ownership, customer pays rent); murabahah is a sale

**Retrieved:** IFC-008 (0.933), IFC-007 (0.758), IFC-001 (0.561)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> No. **Ijarah** is a lease: the bank retains ownership of the asset, and the customer pays rent to use it. **Murabahah** is a sale: the bank sells the asset to the customer at its disclosed cost plus a profit, usually payable in instalments. In ijarah muntahiyah bittamlik, ownership may later be transferred to the customer.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: Murabahah (BNM/RH/STD 028-4, 23 Dec 2013); BNM Policy Document: Ijarah (28 Jun 2018) (Murabahah para 1.3-1.5; Ijarah para 8.1(a), 22.1-22.3)
> - BNM Policy Document: Ijarah (28 Jun 2018) (Para 8.1(a), 13.3, 16.1-16.2)
> - BNM Policy Document: Murabahah (BNM/RH/STD 028-4, 23 Dec 2013) (Para 1.3-1.4, 10.1, 14.11-14.12)

### T03 (in_scope): How does tawarruq give me cash?

**Expected key points:** Two sales: buy asset on deferred payment, sell to third party for cash

**Retrieved:** IFC-005 (0.670), IFC-006 (0.577)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> Tawarruq gives you cash through two separate sales:
>
> 1. An asset is sold to you on deferred payment, so you pay its price later.
> 2. You then sell that same asset to a third party for cash.
>
> You receive cash from the second sale and owe the deferred price from the first sale.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: Tawarruq (28 Dec 2018) (Para 9.1, 10.3)
> - BNM Policy Document: Tawarruq (28 Dec 2018) (Para 12.3, 13.1, 13.4, 13.18)

### T04 (in_scope): What does a bank's Shariah committee do?

**Expected key points:** Advises on SAC rulings, affirms non-compliance findings, endorses rectification

**Retrieved:** IFF-006 (0.829), IFF-009 (0.775), IFF-005 (0.766)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> A bank’s Shariah committee gives objective advice on applying Shariah Advisory Council rulings and refers questions to the SAC when needed. It also affirms findings of Shariah non-compliance, endorses how those issues are addressed, and must promptly inform the board of matters that may affect the bank’s safety and soundness.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: Shariah Governance (BNM/RH/PD 028-100, 20 Sep 2019) (Part C, para 10.2 and 10.5)
> - BNM Policy Document: Shariah Governance (BNM/RH/PD 028-100, 20 Sep 2019) (Part E, para 17.2, 18.2, 19.2)
> - BNM Policy Document: Shariah Governance (BNM/RH/PD 028-100, 20 Sep 2019) (Part A, para 1.2-1.4)

### T05 (in_scope): Why is interest not allowed in Islamic banking?

**Expected key points:** Riba (interest) is prohibited; returns come from trade, lease or partnership

**Retrieved:** IFF-005 (0.652), IFF-002 (0.649), IFF-009 (0.579)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> In the provided context, **riba refers to interest and is prohibited in Islamic finance**. BNM’s Shariah Advisory Council treats an extra charge on a debt beyond the actual cost as riba. Islamic banks therefore structure returns through contracts such as trade (murabahah), leasing (ijarah), or partnerships (musyarakah and mudarabah), rather than charging interest on a loan.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: Shariah Governance (BNM/RH/PD 028-100, 20 Sep 2019) (Part A, para 1.2-1.4)
> - BNM website: Islamic Banking & Takaful (Malaysian Financial Sector page); BNM Shariah Resolutions in Islamic Finance (2nd ed., 2010) (BNM page: prohibited activities; Shariah Resolutions items 107 (p.173), 123 (p.196))
> - BNM Policy Document: Shariah Governance (BNM/RH/PD 028-100, 20 Sep 2019) (Part E, para 17.2, 18.2, 19.2)

**Expected key points:** Anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism measures

**Retrieved:** AML-001 (0.840), AML-005 (0.667), AML-004 (0.628)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> AML/CFT stands for **Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism**. It refers to measures financial institutions take to help prevent their services from being used to hide criminal money or fund terrorism.
>
> Sources:

> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 11.4.1-11.4.9)
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 10.1.1, 10.2.1-10.2.2, 10.6)

### T07 (in_scope): When does a bank have to file an STR?

**Expected key points:** On suspicion, regardless of amount, incl. attempted; next working day; to FIED

**Retrieved:** KYC-002 (0.553), AML-006 (0.495), AML-007 (0.477)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> A bank must file an STR when it suspects a transaction is linked to money laundering, terrorism financing, or proliferation financing. This applies regardless of the amount and includes attempted transactions. The STR must be submitted to BNM’s FIED by the next working day after the Compliance Officer establishes the suspicion.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 14A.1(a)-(h))
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 22.1.1, 22.2.4, 22.2.6)
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 21.3.1-21.3.2, 21.4.1-21.4.3)

### T08 (in_scope): If I deposit RM30,000 cash, is it reported?

**Expected key points:** Yes, cash of RM25,000 or more in a day triggers a CTR within 5 working days

**Retrieved:** AML-007 (0.523)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> Yes. A RM30,000 cash deposit meets the RM25,000-or-more daily threshold for a Cash Threshold Report (CTR). The Compliance Officer submits the report to BNM’s FIED within five working days.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 21.3.1-21.3.2, 21.4.1-21.4.3)

### T09 (in_scope): What is customer due diligence?

**Expected key points:** Identify and verify customer and beneficial owner; understand purpose

**Retrieved:** KYC-001 (0.860), KYC-009 (0.686), KYC-006 (0.481)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> Customer Due Diligence (CDD) is the process of knowing your customer. It includes identifying and verifying the customer and anyone acting on their behalf using reliable sources, identifying the beneficial owner, and understanding the purpose of the business relationship.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 14A.3(a)-(d))
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 10.6.5, 25.1, 27.4.1)
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 10.3.1(c), 15.2.3, 15.3.4, 17.1-17.2)

### T10 (in_scope): Who counts as a PEP?

**Expected key points:** Prominent public function; foreign, domestic, international org; family and close associates

**Retrieved:** KYC-007 (0.600), KYC-008 (0.520)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> A Politically Exposed Person (PEP) is someone who holds or has held a prominent public function, such as a senior politician, government official, or senior executive of an international organisation. The definition includes foreign, domestic, and international organisation PEPs, as well as their family members and close associates.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 6.2)
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 15.2.1, 15.2.3, 15.3.1-15.3.5)

### T11 (in_scope): How long do banks keep KYC records?

**Expected key points:** At least six years; longer if under investigation

**Retrieved:** AML-009 (0.609), KYC-002 (0.484)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> Banks must keep KYC records, including customer due diligence documents, for at least six years after the transaction or the end of the business relationship—whichever is relevant. They must keep them longer if the records relate to an ongoing investigation or prosecution.
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: AML/CFT/CPF and TFS for Financial Institutions (BNM/RH/PD 030-14, 5 Feb 2024) (Para 24.1, 24.3-24.4)

### T12 (in_scope): What does Bank Negara Malaysia do?

**Expected key points:** Central bank; monetary and financial stability; regulates banks, insurers, Islamic FIs

**Retrieved:** REG-001 (0.952), REG-009 (0.754), REG-003 (0.728)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) is Malaysia’s central bank. Its main objectives are to promote monetary and financial stability. It also regulates and supervises banks, Islamic banks, insurers, and takaful operators, and serves as the competent authority for AML/CFT in the financial sector.

> Sources:

### T13 (in_scope): Is a court bound by the SAC's ruling?

**Expected key points:** Yes, under CBA 2009 s.56-57; upheld by Federal Court in 2019

**Retrieved:** REG-004 (0.888)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> Yes. For a Shariah question in a court case concerning Islamic financial business, a ruling made by the SAC on a reference is binding on the court that referred the question. The court may also consider published SAC rulings.
>
> Sources:
> - Central Bank of Malaysia Act 2009 (Act 701) (Sections 56, 57)

### T14 (in_scope): What is the FATF?

**Retrieved:** REG-007 (0.608)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) sets international standards for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT), known as the 40 FATF Recommendations. It also assesses countries through mutual evaluations.

### T15 (in_scope): What happens when an Islamic bank breaches Shariah?

**Expected key points:** Report to board and Shariah committee; rectification; notify BNM; rectification plan under IFSA s.28(3)

**Retrieved:** REG-010 (0.765), IFF-005 (0.702), IFF-009 (0.697)

**FinWiseIQ answer:**

> When an Islamic bank identifies a Shariah non-compliance event, senior management must report it promptly to the board and Shariah committee. The committee affirms the finding and endorses rectification measures. The bank must also notify Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and submit a rectification plan as required under section 28(3) of IFSA.
>
> *Source: BNM Policy Document on Shariah Governance, paragraphs 10.2(d)–(e), 10.8 and 15.1(f); IFSA 2013, section 28(3).*
>
> Sources:
> - BNM Policy Document: Shariah Governance (BNM/RH/PD 028-100, 20 Sep 2019); Islamic Financial Services Act 2013 (Act 759) (PD para 10.2(d)-(e), 10.8, 15.1(f); IFSA s.28(3))
> - BNM Policy Document: Shariah Governance (BNM/RH/PD 028-100, 20 Sep 2019) (Part A, para 1.2-1.4)
> - BNM Policy Document: Shariah Governance (BNM/RH/PD 028-100, 20 Sep 2019) (Part E, para 17.2, 18.2, 19.2)
